extracted.intended_audience: science journalists, researchers, and readers interested in research integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: A blog-style commentary that curates links and reactions about a high-profile scientific retraction (Wakefield/MMR), highlighting investigative findings, journal actions, media coverage, and lessons for science communication and journalism. Useful for those assessing research misconduct, reporting on retractions, or writing about research integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear evidence of data falsification as grounds for retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: “such ‘clear evidence of falsification of data should now close the door on this damaging vaccine scare.’” (BMJ Editor in Chief quoted in the post; BMJ declares article “an elaborate fraud”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is clear evidence that data were falsified, journals should retract the article and publicly characterize the work accordingly; strong language (e.g., likening to Piltdown Man) may be used to communicate the severity. The post points to the BMJ press release, editorial, feature, and online analysis as the appropriate institutional response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate misconduct from honest error
rubrics_metrics.description: “While most retractions don't involve fraud, many involve misconduct.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a retraction arises from honest mistakes or from deliberate misconduct — the latter has different implications for institutional response, public communication, and investigation depth. Investigations often 'peel back layers' and reveal important stories about conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative journalism's role in uncovering fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: “The investigation by Brian Deer in the BMJ is yet more proof that scientific retractions are worth watching.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent long-form investigative work can uncover data problems, ethical breaches, or fraud that lead to retraction; journalism can be a primary driver in exposing misconduct (examples cited: Brian Deer on Wakefield; Adam breaking Scott Reuben's fraud).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal response should include retraction plus explanatory editorial/analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: BMJ published multiple items: a retraction, an editorial, a feature, and online analysis (press release likening the work to a hoax).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For high-profile misconduct, journals should not only retract but also provide transparent editorial explanation and follow-up analysis to explain the reasons, context, and implications for readers and the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate ethical and methodological failings explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: The post links to resources (e.g., video “Vaccines: A Measured Response”) examining the paper's ethical and methodological failings for a non-technical audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess research for ethical breaches (e.g., consent, IRB issues) and methodological problems (study design, data handling) and communicate these failings clearly to technical and non-technical audiences; use accessible analyses to explain why a study is invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate risk responsibly to avoid amplifying myths
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to a piece on 'what we can learn from the fiasco about communicating risk.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting on retractions tied to public health, avoid inadvertently amplifying myths or fears; provide context about absolute and relative risks, and explain why the scientific consensus stands despite a retracted paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misrepresenting affected communities in media coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: “The news coverage in the US has (perhaps inadvertently) perpetrated the idea that all parents of children with autism believe in the vaccine causation myth. It is a complete falsehood.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage should not generalize the beliefs of a whole community; recognize diversity of views among affected groups (e.g., many parents and adults with autism robustly reject the vaccine causation myth). Use precise language and representative sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage embargoes and disclose breaches transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: Embargo Watch examined whether a tweet — and later, CNN — broke the embargo on the BMJ articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists and outlets should respect embargoes where agreed, and if breaches occur they should be disclosed and discussed; embargo handling can affect the release, framing, and reception of investigative findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curate coverage to add value when many accounts exist
rubrics_metrics.description: “The web leaves us free to curate as well as create.” The post primarily curates links and suggested commentary rather than repeating all coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story has extensive prior coverage, add value by curating the best analyses, providing synthesis, and highlighting diverse perspectives rather than duplicating material; curation is a valid contribution for commentators and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose relevant personal relationships or potential conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Author disclosure: 'Mnookin — a friend of Ivan’s from college — was on CNN... (More disclosure: Ivan’s wife works as a writer/producer at AC360.)'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and journalists should disclose relevant relationships, friendships, or employment ties that could be perceived to influence coverage or commentary; concise transparency helps maintain credibility.
